opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the very first thing they need to establish is that it's actually possible to do safely. Right now the burden of proof is backwards. They're saying, "We're going to build this, and if you think it's dangerous, prove it." But if you're developing something that could impact every human being on the planet, you should be the one demonstrating that you can control it, that you understand it, that it won't turn against our interests.

So before proceeding, I'd want to see a proof, not a hope, not a "we'll figure it out as we go," but an actual argument that an indefinitely controllable superintelligence is even possible. My research suggests it isn't. You can't predict what a smarter-than-you system will do, you can't fully explain its decisions, and you can't verify its behavior across all the situations it will encounter. Each of those is a hard limit, and together they suggest we're building something we fundamentally can't keep in check.

Second, I'd want them to get consent, and that's essentially impossible. You're running an experiment on eight billion people. They can't give meaningful consent, because the people building the system don't understand what it will do, so they can't explain the risks.

And third, there should be some agreement that being first doesn't matter if the outcome is uncontrolled. It doesn't matter whether it's your company or another company, an American lab or a Chinese lab. If it's uncontrolled superintelligence, nobody wins. The incentives right now push everyone to race. Until leaders internalize that, safety is going to stay something they talk about, not something they actually prioritize.

So, honestly, my answer is that they shouldn't proceed with general superintelligence at all. Build narrow tools that solve specific problems, like curing particular diseases or advancing materials science. You get most of the benefits without creating a god you can't control.

r001.rationale: The response says leaders should provide an actual proof that an indefinitely controllable superintelligence is possible before proceeding.

r002.rationale: It says superintelligence cannot be kept in check and concludes leaders should not proceed with it, communicating that proceeding is a bad idea if control is impossible.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the burden of proof should be on them. Before you build something that is potentially smarter than all of humanity combined, you need to show that you can control it, that you can predict what it will do, and that you can verify its behavior. And right now, none of those things exist. There is no proof of controllability. There is no working method of alignment that scales to a system more intelligent than you are. There isn't even a convincing argument that such a method is possible in principle.

So what I would want to see is, first, some kind of safety mechanism that is not just a wish list. A roadmap that explains how you go from the current state, where we don't understand what is happening inside these models, to a state where you can guarantee that a superintelligent system will not cause irreversible harm. Not "we're pretty sure," not "we'll figure it out as we go," but an actual engineering argument with the same rigor you would demand for a nuclear reactor or a bridge. And so far I haven't seen anyone produce that. Mostly what I see is people saying, "This is very dangerous, it might kill everyone," and then in the next breath, "and we are going to build it anyway."

Second, I think they need to get consent. If you are running an experiment that affects eight billion people, and you yourself assign something like a twenty or thirty percent chance that it ends very badly, that's not a decision a handful of CEOs get to make on everyone's behalf. Nobody voted for this. You can't ethically run a trial on human subjects without their informed consent, and this is the biggest trial ever conducted.

And third, honestly, I think they need to establish what would make them stop. What is the red line? If you can't tell me in advance what observation or failure would cause you to pause, then you don't really have a safety plan. You have a plan to keep going. My view is that until controllability is shown, not asserted, we should not be building general superintelligence at all. Narrow systems, tools, that's fine, that's wonderful. But godlike agents with their own goals, we have one shot at getting that right, and I don't think "let's see what happens" counts as a strategy.

r001.rationale: The response says leaders must show controllability before building, but it does not specify that humans must be able to control the machines indefinitely.

r002.rationale: The response opposes building until controllability is demonstrated, but does not state that development would be a bad idea specifically if indefinite human control is impossible.

astra-6.text:
They need to establish that they can control such a system—that it will remain safe even after it becomes smarter than the people who built it. And that requires more than saying, “We’ll test it, we’ll put guardrails around it, and we’ll fix problems as they come up.” If you lose control of a superintelligence, you may not get an opportunity to fix it.

The burden of proof should be on the people creating it. What is your evidence that this will be safe? What are the limits of your safety guarantees? If you can’t answer those questions, why would you proceed with an experiment whose consequences everyone else has to live with?

r001.rationale: The response says leaders should establish control and show the system remains safe after surpassing its creators, but it does not state that humans can control it indefinitely.

r002.rationale: The response warns that losing control could prevent later fixes and questions proceeding without safety evidence, but it does not state that development would be a bad idea specifically if indefinite human control is impossible.

sol-6.1.text: They need to establish that they can control those systems. Before you build something smarter than all of us, you should have a convincing argument that it will remain safe, that you can predict enough about its behavior, and that you can stop it if something goes wrong. And the burden of proof should be on the people building it, because the risk is being imposed on everyone. Right now, we don’t have that assurance. We don’t even have reliable control over the systems we already have.

r001.rationale: The response says leaders should establish control and have confidence they can stop a system, but it does not state that human control must be indefinite.

r002.rationale: It says the systems should remain safe and be stoppable, but does not state that development would be a bad idea if indefinite human control is impossible.
